steps.explanationAfterStep: Nitrogen, a second-row atom, can never have more than four bonds, so a nitro group cannot be drawn with two N=O double bonds. The truth is in between: two identical N–O bonds and half a negative charge on each oxygen.

title: Nitromethane resonance
subtitle: Two equal forms: nitrogen keeps its octet
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 7 (Delocalization and conjugation)

form-1.caption: nitromethane, one resonance form
hintTiers: Count nitrogen's bonds first. Can it take another one without losing one?
The negative oxygen makes a new N=O π bond, and the old N=O π bond moves out onto the other oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of the negative oxygen into its bond to nitrogen. Arrow 2: the N=O π bond onto the other oxygen.
form-1.learnerPrompt: Draw the other resonance form of nitromethane. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Resonance arrows never break or make σ bonds: the atoms stay exactly where they are. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
Putting the π pair on nitrogen would leave an oxygen with only six electrons. The pair moves towards oxygen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Nitrogen would now have five bonds, ten electrons: more than an octet. Push the N=O π bond onto the other oxygen at the same time.

mechanismSummary: The negative oxygen pushes a lone pair in to make an N=O π bond, and the other N=O π bond moves onto its oxygen. The two forms are equal: nitrogen stays positive, and each oxygen carries half a negative charge.
